Paleomagnetic and geochronological results of the Risong Formation in the
western Lhasa Terrane: Insights into the Lhasa-Qiangtang collision and
stratal age
Suo Wanga,b, Tianshui Yanga,b,*, Feng Gaoa,b, Weiwei Biana,b,c, Jingjie Jina,b,
Wenxiao Penga,b, Xianwei Jiaoa,b, Jiahui Maa,b, Shihong Zhanga,b, Huaichun Wua, Haiyan Lia,
Liwan Caoa
aState Key Laboratory of Biogeology and Environmental Geology, China University of Geosciences, Beijing 100083, China
bSchool of Earth Sciences and Resources, China University of Geosciences, Beijing 100083, China
cState Key Laboratory of Lithospheric Evolution, Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100029, China
A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T
Editor: Howard Falcon-Lang To constrain the Lhasa-Qiangtang collisional age, a combined paleomagnetic and geochronologic investigation
has been performed on the Risong Formation redbeds and volcanic rocks in the Wuma area of the western Lhasa
Keywords: terrane (LT). A U-Pb dating result from the volcanic interlayer at the bottom of the Risong Formation redbeds
Bangong-Nujiang suture zone yields the youngest weighted mean 206Pb/238U age of 110.6 ±1.3 Ma, and the two detrital zircon U-Pb chro-
Meso-Tethyan evolution nological results from the Risong Formation redbeds provide the youngest weighted mean 206Pb/238U age of
Zircon U-Pb geochronology 106.9 ±3.3 Ma (the top strata of section A) and 120.5 ±3.0 Ma (the top strata of section D), respectively. Our
Inclination discrepancy
new geochronological results suggest that the studied Risong Formation redbeds formed during the Early
Cretaceous, rather than during the Late Jurassic as assigned by 1:250,000 scale Wuma regional geological survey
report. Characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) directions from two different limbs of folds concentrate in
two different groups, and both site-mean directions pass positive fold tests. One group including 32 sites yields a
tilt-corrected site-mean direction that is D =356.1◦, I =33.1◦with α 95 =2.3◦, corresponding to a paleopole at
75.2◦N, 278.1◦E with dp/dm =1.5◦/2.6◦ and a paleolatitude of 18.1◦ ±1.5◦N for the study area (32.41◦N,
83.39◦E). The other group including 24 sites provides a tilt-corrected site-mean direction that is D =60.5◦, I =
48.5◦with α 9 5 =2.0◦, corresponding to a paleopole at 38.7◦N, 159.6◦E with dp/dm =1.7◦/2.6◦and a paleo-
latitude of 29.5◦±1.7◦N for the study area (32.41◦N, 83.39◦E). After syntectonic-sedimentation-correction, the
Fisherian site-mean inclination of 41.7◦±1.6◦and corresponding paleolatitude of 24.0◦±1.2◦N obtained from
56 sites of two different limbs are consistent with the inclination-only mean of 39.6 ±3.1◦and corresponding
paleolatitude of 22.5◦±2.2◦N deduced from the ChRM directions of all the 56 paleomagnetic sites, suggesting
that the observed inclination discrepancy of the Risong Formation redbeds may result from the syntectonic
sedimentation. Comparing the Early Cretaceous paleolatitudes observed from the western LT with those from the
western Qiangtang terrane shows insignificant paleolatitude difference, supporting that the Lhasa-Qiangtang
collision in the western part occurred at or before the Early Cretaceous.

A total of 56 paleomagnetic sites were collected from four sections interlayer within the Risong Fm redbeds located at the paleomagnetic
near the Wuma town, which is about 70 km west of the county of Gerze site WM1 of the section A.
(Fig. 1). Twenty-four sites including 248 core samples were collected
from section A (WM1–17 and WM35–41; 32◦24′36′′N, 83◦23′08′′E, 3. Laboratory procedures and methods
4622 m), where the bedding dips are about 61–70◦ toward the north-
west (Fig. 3). It should be noted that there is a basaltic interlayer at the Standard oriented cores were cut into 2.2-cm-long specimens for
bottom of section A and 10 specimens of WM1 were sampled from the further tests. To clarify the magnetic carriers and choose the proper
basalt. The remaining 32 paleomagnetic sites including 327 core sam- demagnetization procedure, the isothermal remanent magnetization
ples were drilled from the sections B (WM18–21, WM46–47; (IRM), back-field demagnetization of saturation IRM and three-axis IRM
32 ◦ 24 ′ 03 ′′ N, 83 ◦ 35 ′ 19 ′′ E, 4536 m), C (WM22–26 and WM48–52; were acquired by an ASC IM10–30 pulse magnetizer, and the IRM was
measured by an AGICO JR–6A spinner magnetometer. The three-axis
IRM was imparted in successively smaller fields of 2.4 T, 0.4 T, and
0.12 T along three mutually orthogonal directions (Lowrie, 1990). To
avoid the influence of heating, we performed the anisotropy of magnetic
susceptibility (AMS) measurement by using an AGICO MFK1 Kappa-
bridge before thermal demagnetization.
Stepwise thermal demagnetization up to 580 ◦C for volcanic speci-
mens and 680 ◦C for redbeds specimens was conducted using a Magnetic
Measurements Thermal Demagnetiser Super Cooling (MMTDSC)
furnace or an ASC–TD 48 furnace, and remanences were measured using
the 2G-755-4K cryogenic magnetometer. Thermal demagnetization
temperature intervals were 100–50 ◦C below 500 ◦C and shifted to
20–10 ◦C above 500 ◦C. All thermal demagnetization and remanent
magnetization measurements were performed in the magnetically
shielded room (< 300 nT) at the Paleomagnetism and Environmental
Magnetism Laboratory (PEML), China University of Geosciences, Beijing
(CUGB). Characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) directions were
gained using principal component analysis (Kirschvink, 1980) from at
least 5 successive thermal demagnetization steps. Site-mean directions
were calculated using Fisherian statistics (Fisher, 1953). Paleomagnetic
data were analyzed using the computer program packages developed by
Enkin (1990) and Cogn´e (2003).
A total of 13 standard core samples were drilled from hand blocks in
the direction perpendicular to the strata bedding, and then these stan-
dard 2.5-cm-diameter core samples were further cut into 2.2-cm-long
specimens. The IRM parallel (IRMx) and perpendicular (IRMz) were
obtained at a 45◦ angle to the strata bedding plane by using an ASC
IM10–30 pulse magnetizer, and then measured by using a JR-6 spinner
magnetometer every step. After the IRM obtained to 1000 mT, the
stepwise thermal demagnetization was performed by using an MMTDSC.
To further clarify the micro texture and composition of the iron ox-
ides, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) observations and energy
dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) analyses for a few typical specimens of
the Risong Fm redbeds were performed at the Institute of Geology and
Geophysics, China Academy of Sciences.
Zircon grains from three block samples were selected at the Langfang
Gengxin Geological Service Company. Cathodoluminescence (CL) pho-

4. Results
4.1. Zircon U-Pb analytical results
CL images showed that the checked zircon grains were euhedral to
subhedral with clear oscillatory zoning, indicating that zircons were
magmatic in origin. The volcanic sample collected from the paleomag-
netic site WM1 provided a youngest weighted mean 206Pb/238U age of
110.6 ±1.3 Ma, and the two sandstone samples from the paleomagnetic
sites of WM36 and WM55 yielded the youngest weighted mean
206Pb/238U ages of 106.9 ±3.3 Ma and 120.5 ±3.0 Ma, respectively
(Fig. 4). These three new zircon LA-ICP-MS U-Pb dating results show
that the sampled Risong Fm redbeds in the Wuma area formed during
the Early Cretaceous (~120.5–106.9 Ma).
4.2. AMS results
The equal-area projections of the maximum (K1), intermediate (K2)
and minimum (K3) principal axes after bedding correction were shown
in Fig. 5. For most specimens, their K1 and K2 AMS directions were
almost parallel to the bedding, and their K1 directions grouped in a
northwest-southeast direction. Although the K3 AMS directions of most
specimens were basically perpendicular to bedding plane, they started to
trend a girdle distribution along the northeast-southwest direction.
Furthermore, the values of AMS degree (Pj) were relatively low (most Pj
<1.05), and the shape parameters of AMS ellipsoid (T) oscillated stably
around a mean value (T =0.085). The AMS ellipsoid showed a transition
stage between oblate and prolate. These AMS characteristics can be
classified into incipient deformation stage to weak cleavage stage (Par´es
et al., 1999; Par´es, 2015; Hrouda and Chadima, 2020), and also are
consistent with a weak and moderate deformed magnetic fabric (Weil
and Yonkee, 2009). These AMS results, combined with that field out-
crops (Fig. 3) and the following microscopic observations in Section 4.4,
support that the sampled Risong Fm redbeds did not suffer from strong
deformation.
4.3. Rock magnetic results
The IRM acquisition curve of the typical basalt specimen revealed a
rapid increase below 0.1 T, and saturation was fully reached at ~0.5 T
(Fig. 6A). When the backfield demagnetization was performed, the
remanent magnetization decreased rapidly and the maximum coercive Fig. 6. A, C, E, G. IRM acquisition curves and back-field demagnetization of
SIRM curves of representative samples. B, D, F, H. Thermal demagnetization of
three orthogonal IRM curves of representative samples.
force was less than 60 mT (Fig. 6A), indicating that low-coercivity
magnetic carriers were dominant. Stepwise thermal demagnetization
of three orthogonal IRM components (Lowrie, 1990) showed that all the
soft, medium and hard components were unblocked at ~580 ◦C
(Fig. 6B). These results revealed that magnetite was dominant magnetic
carriers in studied basaltic rocks.
For the representative redbeds specimens, the IRM acquisition curves
increased steadily until 2.4 T where the saturation was not fully ach-
ieved yet (Fig. 6C, E, G). When reverse fields were applied, the rema-
nence decreased rapidly and reduced to zero at 0.3–0.5 T (Fig. 6C, E, G),
figuring that the existence of high-coercivity magnetic carriers. The
Lowrie (1990) test showed that the hard, medium and soft components
were unblocked at ~680 ◦C, and the soft component revealed a clear
inflection point at ~580 ◦C (Fig. 6D, F, H). These results indicated that
hematite was the main magnetic carrier in the studied redbeds, and that
magnetite should also be present.

the sampling location; Plat and Plon, latitude and longitude of the pole; A95, the radius that the mean pole lies within 95% confidence; dp/dm, semiaxes of elliptical
error of the pole at a probability of 95%; paleolat, paleolatitude calculated for the reference point at (32.41◦N, 83.39◦E) for the western LT and the western QT; n/N,
number of samples/sites used to calculate Fisher mean; Test, the paleomagnetic data has passed field test; F, positive fold test; R, positive reversal test; D, dual-polarity;
